crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting a Manuscript
children.blurb: Drafting a manuscript in academic writing covers turning research findings, data, and argument into a structured paper suitable for submission to a journal or conference.

children.name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review means using structured critique to find weak premises, unsupported claims, alternative explanations, and logical gaps in a manuscript before submitting to a journal.

children.name: Disciplinary Register and Language
children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language covers the specialized vocabulary, grammatical patterns, rhetorical conventions, and citation habits that distinguish academic fields from one another.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: Plagiarism and AI detection covers identifying copied text, paraphrased material without attribution, and machine-generated prose in manuscripts, student work, and peer review.

children.name: Explaining Research After Publication
children.blurb: Explaining research after publication covers the work of turning a finished paper into clear summaries, annotations, and discussions for readers beyond the original authors.

sections.body: Academic writing and peer review in AI covers the practical use of machine learning systems to draft, revise, check, and explain scholarly manuscripts. Right now, researchers use large language models to generate section drafts, rephrase sentences, suggest alternative phrasings, and produce plain language summaries of completed papers. Tools also compare a manuscript against large text corpora to flag passages that closely match published work, and some systems attempt to predict whether an argument will survive reviewer scrutiny by looking for missing citations or weak transitions. This is not a theoretical field; it is a set of working practices built on models that already produce text and similarity scores in everyday research workflows.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The solved parts are narrow: grammar correction, sentence-level rewriting, reference formatting, and basic similarity detection work well enough to save time. What is not solved is anything that requires judgment about truth, novelty, or disciplinary fit. A model can draft a plausible methods section but cannot verify that the described experiment actually happened, and it cannot tell whether a result is important. Plagiarism detectors produce scores, not verdicts, and they regularly miss paraphrased ideas or flag common phrases as copied. The honest limit is that current AI assists with the surface of writing and checking, while the core of peer review, deciding whether a claim is sound and whether the evidence supports it, remains a human task.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages under this section follow a manuscript from first draft to public explanation. Drafting a Manuscript is the starting point for turning notes and results into a complete first version, with attention to structure and section order. Testing Arguments Before Peer Review then helps a researcher probe the logic and anticipate reviewer objections before submission. Disciplinary Register and Language addresses the harder problem of matching the expected tone, terminology, and citation habits of a specific field, which generic drafting tools often get wrong. Plagiarism and AI Detection explains what current similarity and AI writing detectors actually measure, including their false positive and false negative patterns. Explaining Research After Publication covers the later stage of writing lay summaries, press releases, or social media threads that make a finished paper understandable to readers outside the original review process.
